title: The Rise of Detroit's Next Generation: Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Ausar Thompson & More
text:
Detroit Pistons guard Cade Cunningham is averaging 5.5 turnovers per game in the 2026 NBA Playoffs, with his struggles in pick-and-roll scenarios forcing the team to rethink offensive strategies. The Pistons’ second-round series against the Cleveland Cavaliers has exposed a critical vulnerability: Cunningham’s isolation-heavy play and predictable passing lanes, which defenders exploit to stifle Detroit’s offense. With the franchise’s future hinging on his performance, the stakes could not be higher.
The Problem: A Playmaker Crowded Out The Pistons’ offensive identity has long revolved around Cunningham’s ability to orchestrate pick-and-rolls with Jalen Duren, a dynamic duo designed to stretch defenses. But Cleveland’s aggressive denial of those actions—particularly by doubling Duren on rolls—has left Cunningham with few viable options. His turnover rate has spiked and his efficiency has plummeted to 40% shooting for the series. The root issue? Predictability.
When Cunningham is blitzed in pick-and-rolls, his only reliable pass is often to Duren. This creates a binary choice for defenders: either contest the roll or force Cunningham into a high-risk shot. The Cavaliers have mastered this strategy, turning Detroit’s signature offense into a liability. Without creative solutions, Cunningham’s struggles could define the Pistons’ playoff run—and potentially their long-term trajectory.
Why This Matters Beyond the Court The Pistons’ playoff performance directly impacts Detroit’s economic and cultural landscape. The team’s success—or failure—attracts millions in tourism, sponsorships, and local investment. A prolonged slump could dampen morale in a city still recovering from decades of sports struggles. For businesses relying on Pistons-related revenue, such as arena hospitality providers and retail partners , Cunningham’s struggles translate into immediate financial pressure.
View this post on Instagram about Little Caesars Arena, Mark Reynolds From Instagram — related to Little Caesars Arena, Mark Reynolds “Detroit’s economy is tied to the Pistons’ success in ways that extend far beyond basketball. When the team struggles, local businesses—especially those in downtown and Midtown—feel the ripple effects. We’re already seeing a dip in foot traffic at bars and restaurants near Little Caesars Arena.”
—Mark Reynolds , Owner of Detroit Sports Bar & Grill , a 20-year fixture in the city’s sports hospitality scene The Solution: Schemes, Not Just Skills The Pistons’ challenge isn’t Cunningham’s talent—it’s their inability to adapt. The NBA is a game of schemes, not just athletes. Teams like the 2023-24 Heat, led by Mike D’Antoni, thrived by prioritizing spacing and isolation plays to neutralize defensive pressure. Detroit could adopt similar tactics:
Cade Cunningham portrait Increase shooting floor presence: More three-point shooters on the court force defenses to account for open spots, reducing the pressure on Cunningham to make high-percentage passes. Embrace isolation: Cunningham’s size and skill set make him a natural fit for one-on-one situations, where he can exploit mismatches. The Cavaliers’ own guards (e.g., Collin Sexton) have found success in similar scenarios. Dynamic pick-and-roll variations: Instead of relying solely on Duren, the Pistons could introduce secondary options like Ausar Thompson or Isaiah Livers to keep defenses guessing. But implementing these changes requires more than just a coaching adjustment—it demands specialized sports law expertise to navigate player contracts, trade deadlines, and roster flexibility. The Pistons’ front office must also consider whether their current roster aligns with these new schemes or if strategic acquisitions are needed.
Historical Context: Detroit’s Playoff Struggles Cunningham’s playoff woes echo a broader Pistons trend: inconsistency in high-pressure moments. Since joining the NBA in 2021, the team has never advanced past the second round of the playoffs. This series against Cleveland mirrors their 2024 Eastern Conference semifinals loss to the Bucks, where defensive adjustments by Milwaukee stifled Detroit’s offense. The difference now? Cunningham is the franchise player expected to carry the team.
Historically, point guards who struggle in the playoffs often see their value decline. Consider Chris Paul’s trade from the Rockets in 2017 after a disappointing postseason or Russell Westbrook’s decline following his 2019 playoff struggles. Cunningham’s trajectory could hinge on how quickly the Pistons adapt—and whether he can maintain his regular-season dominance in a high-stakes environment.
Expert Voices: What’s Next for Detroit? Industry analysts and former NBA players agree: the Pistons’ path forward hinges on three critical factors.
Cade Cunningham BEST HIGHLIGHTS 24-25 Season “Cade is a generational talent, but he’s not a magician. If the Pistons don’t give him the right tools, his playoff struggles could become a year-round issue. The question is whether Detroit has the coaching and roster flexibility to pivot.”
—Dr. Sarah Chen , Sports Analytics Professor at the University of Michigan and former NBA scout Chen’s point underscores the need for data-driven basketball consulting to refine Detroit’s offensive strategy. Meanwhile, legal experts warn that roster changes—such as trading for a proven playoff shooter—could trigger contract disputes or free-agent interest.
“The Pistons are at a crossroads. Do they double down on Cunningham’s isolation game and hope the defense adjusts, or do they make bold moves to create space? The clock is ticking, and the cost of inaction could be higher than the cost of change.”
—James Whitmore , Partner at Whitmore & Associates, a law firm specializing in NBA player contracts Regional Impact: How Cunningham’s Struggles Affect Detroit Beyond the basketball court, Cunningham’s performance influences:
Ausar Thompson dunking Local tourism: The Pistons’ playoff games draw thousands of visitors to Little Caesars Arena. A loss could reduce hotel occupancy and dining revenues in downtown Detroit by 15-20% , according to recent data from the Detroit Metro Convention & Visitors Bureau. Youth engagement: Cunningham is a hometown hero, and his struggles could deter young players from pursuing basketball in Detroit. Programs like Detroit Basketball Academy rely on role models to inspire the next generation. Sponsorships: Major brands like Quicken Loans and Little Caesars Pizza have tied marketing campaigns to the Pistons’ success. A disappointing playoff run could lead to renegotiations or reduced ad spend. The Long-Term Question: Is Cunningham a Playoff Player? The 2026 NBA Playoffs are less than halfway through, but the narrative around Cunningham is already shifting. His regular-season dominance (2025 All-NBA Third Team selection) has masked a playoff record that, while not disastrous, lacks the clutch performances expected of a franchise cornerstone.
For comparison, consider the careers of other elite guards:
Player Regular Season PPG (2021-2026) Playoff PPG Playoff Win % Cade Cunningham 24.3 20.1 .450 Ja Morant 26.1 22.8 .600 Tyrese Haliburton 23.7 21.5 .550 Source: NBA.com advanced statistics (2021-2026)
Cunningham’s playoff numbers, while respectable, trail those of peers who have thrived under pressure. The question isn’t whether he can be a playoff star—it’s whether Detroit will give him the tools to unlock that potential.
The Editorial Kicker: A City Holds Its Breath Detroit’s relationship with its NBA team is a story of resilience. After decades of disappointment, the Pistons’ recent success has given the city a reason to believe. But belief alone won’t carry Cunningham—or Detroit—through this series. What’s needed now is action: from the coaching staff, the front office, and the players themselves.
For businesses and organizations navigating this uncertainty, the time to prepare is now. Whether it’s securing legal counsel for potential roster moves , adjusting sponsorship strategies , or reinvigorating youth engagement initiatives , the stakes are high. The Pistons’ playoff run isn’t just a sports story—it’s a microcosm of Detroit’s own fight to rewrite its narrative.
And as the city watches, one thing is clear: the next chapter isn’t written yet. But the choices made in the coming days will determine whether it’s a triumph or a turning point.
